hmmt-feb-2005-team2-01.title: Count the possible types
hmmt-feb-2005-team2-01.body:
A domino of type $(a,b)$, $0\le a\le b$, $(a,b)\ne(0,0)$, fits in the $m\times n$ array iff it can be placed with offsets $a$ along one side and $b$ along the other. Since $m\le n$, the domino fits iff $a\le m-1$ and $b\le n-1$: if it fits the other way ($b\le m-1$, $a\le n-1$) then also $a\le b\le m-1$ and $b\le m-1\le n-1$. So the types are the pairs $(a,b)$ with $0\le a\le m-1$, $a\le b\le n-1$, excluding $(0,0)$. For each $a=0,\dots,m-1$ there are $n-a$ values of $b$, so the number of types is
$$\sum_{a=0}^{m-1}(n-a)-1=mn-\frac{m(m-1)}2-1=\frac{2mn-m^2+m-2}2.$$

**Answer: $mn-\dfrac{m(m-1)}2-1$**

hmmt-feb-2005-team2-02.title: Construction
hmmt-feb-2005-team2-02.body:
If $a=0$, a $1\times2b$ rectangle is tileable: pair the cell in column $c$ with the cell in column $c+b$ for $c=1,\dots,b$. If $a>0$, a $2a\times2b$ rectangle is tileable: split it into four $a\times b$ quarters and pair each cell with the corresponding cell of the diagonally opposite quarter (offset $(a,b)$). The area is $2b\max\{1,2a\}$; the next problem shows that no tileable rectangle can have smaller dimensions.

**Answer: $\max\{1,2a\}\times2b$**

hmmt-feb-2005-team2-03.title: Look at the central square
hmmt-feb-2005-team2-03.body:
Let the rectangle have $p$ rows and $q$ columns (numbered from $0$) and be $(a,b)$-tileable. Take the square in row $r=\lfloor\frac{p-1}2\rfloor$ and column $s=\lfloor\frac{q-1}2\rfloor$. Then $\max(r,p-1-r)=\lfloor p/2\rfloor$ and $\max(s,q-1-s)=\lfloor q/2\rfloor$: no square of the rectangle is more than $\lfloor p/2\rfloor$ rows or $\lfloor q/2\rfloor$ columns away from it.

In the tiling this square has a partner whose offset is $(\pm x,\pm y)$ with $(x,y)=(a,b)$ or $(b,a)$. The partner lies in the rectangle, so $x\le\lfloor p/2\rfloor$ and $y\le\lfloor q/2\rfloor$, i.e. $p\ge2x$ and $q\ge2y$. Hence either $p\ge2a,\ q\ge2b$ or $p\ge2b,\ q\ge2a$; together with $p,q\ge1$ this says the rectangle contains a $\max\{1,2a\}\times2b$ rectangle in one of the two orientations. $\blacksquare$

hmmt-feb-2005-team2-04.title: Coloring for necessity, blocks for sufficiency
hmmt-feb-2005-team2-04.body:
($\Leftarrow$) If $2b\mid m$ and $2b\mid n$, cut the rectangle into $2b\times2b$ squares. In each, split into four $b\times b$ quarters and pair each cell with the corresponding cell of the diagonally opposite quarter (offset $(b,\pm b)$).

($\Rightarrow$) Color the first $b$ rows black, the next $b$ rows white, the next $b$ black, and so on. A $(b,b)$ domino changes the row by exactly $b$, so it covers one black and one white square. Hence a tileable rectangle has equally many black and white squares, i.e. equally many black rows and white rows. Write $m=2bq+t$ with $0\le t<2b$: the first $2bq$ rows balance, and the last $t$ rows are $\min(t,b)$ black rows followed by $\max(0,t-b)$ white rows. For $0<t\le b$ this leaves $t>0$ extra black rows; for $b<t<2b$ it leaves $b-(t-b)=2b-t>0$ extra black rows. So balance forces $t=0$. So $2b\mid m$. By symmetry (color columns) $2b\mid n$. $\blacksquare$

hmmt-feb-2005-team2-05.title: Both directions
hmmt-feb-2005-team2-05.body:
($\Leftarrow$) Say $2b\mid m$ (the other case is symmetric). Cut the rectangle into horizontal strips of $2b$ rows. In a strip pair $(r,c)$ with $(r+b,c)$ for $r=0,\dots,b-1$ (offset $(b,0)$).

($\Rightarrow$) Assume $2b\nmid m$ and $2b\nmid n$. Number rows and columns from $0$. For residues $(\rho,\sigma)\in\{0,\dots,b-1\}^2$ let $K_{\rho\sigma}$ be the set of squares whose row is $\equiv\rho$ and column $\equiv\sigma\pmod b$; it is an $m_\rho\times n_\sigma$ array (in the rows $\rho,\rho+b,\dots$ and columns $\sigma,\sigma+b,\dots$) with $m_\rho\in\{\lfloor m/b\rfloor,\lceil m/b\rceil\}$. A $(0,b)$ domino joins two squares in the same class, adjacent in that class's array. So a tiling restricts to an ordinary domino tiling of every $K_{\rho\sigma}$, which requires $m_\rho n_\sigma$ to be even.

Now choose $\rho$ with $m_\rho$ odd: if $b\nmid m$, both $\lfloor m/b\rfloor$ and $\lceil m/b\rceil$ occur as $m_\rho$ (they are consecutive integers, so one is odd); if $b\mid m$, then $m_\rho=m/b$ is odd because $2b\nmid m$. Likewise choose $\sigma$ with $n_\sigma$ odd. Then $K_{\rho\sigma}$ has odd area and cannot be tiled by dominoes, a contradiction. $\blacksquare$

hmmt-feb-2005-team2-06.title: Residue classes
hmmt-feb-2005-team2-06.body:
For residues $(ho,\sigma)$ modulo $k$ consider the squares with row $\equivho$ and column $\equiv\sigma\pmod k$. Both squares of an $(a,b)$ domino lie in the same class, since their offsets $a,b$ are multiples of $k$. In the class, which is an $m'	imes n'$ array with $m'\in\{\lfloor m/kfloor,\lceil m/kceil\}$ and $n'\in\{\lfloor n/kfloor,\lceil n/kceil\}$, the domino has offsets $ rac ak, rac bk$ (so it is an $(a/k,b/k)$ domino). A tiling therefore tiles each class array by dominoes, so each class has an even number $m'n'$ of squares.

Suppose $2k
mid m$ and $2k
mid n$. If $k
mid m$, both $\lfloor m/kfloor$ and $\lceil m/kceil$ occur as $m'$ (for different residues $ho$) and, being consecutive, one is odd; if $k\mid m$, then $m'=m/k$ is odd because $2k
mid m$. So some class has $m'$ odd, and similarly some $\sigma$ gives $n'$ odd; the class $(ho,\sigma)$ then has $m'n'$ odd, impossible. Hence $2k\mid m$ or $2k\mid n$. $ lacksquare$

hmmt-feb-2005-team2-07.title: Factor $x^{12}-1$
hmmt-feb-2005-team2-07.body:
$x^{12}-1=(x^6-1)(x^6+1)=(x^3-1)(x^3+1)(x^6+1)=(x-1)(x^2+x+1)(x+1)(x^2-x+1)(x^2+1)(x^4-x^2+1)$ (using $x^6+1=(x^2+1)(x^4-x^2+1)$). All twelfth roots of unity are roots of this product, and the factors of degree $1$ and $2$ account for the roots of orders $1,2,3,4,6$ (these are $\pm1$, the primitive cube roots, the primitive sixth roots and $\pm i$): that is $8$ roots. The remaining $4$ roots, the primitive twelfth roots $e^{\pm i\pi/6},e^{\pm5i\pi/6}$, are the roots of $x^4-x^2+1$.

This quartic has integer coefficients. It is irreducible over $\mathbb Q$: it has no real roots, so any factorization into quadratics would pair the roots into complex-conjugate pairs, giving $x^2-\sqrt3x+1$ and $x^2+\sqrt3x+1$ with irrational coefficients, and $x^4-x^2+1$ has no rational root.

**Answer: $x^4-x^2+1$**

hmmt-feb-2005-team2-08.title: Conjugation
hmmt-feb-2005-team2-08.body:
Since $|x|=|y|=1$, $\bar x=\frac1x$ and $\bar y=\frac1y$. Then
$$\overline{(x+y)^k}=\left(\frac1x+\frac1y\right)^k=\left(\frac{x+y}{xy}\right)^k=\frac{(x+y)^k}{(xy)^k}=(x+y)^k,$$
because $(xy)^k=x^ky^k=1$. A complex number equal to its conjugate is real. $\blacksquare$

hmmt-feb-2005-team2-08.title: Geometry
hmmt-feb-2005-team2-08.body: The argument of each of $x,y$ is a multiple of $\frac{2\pi}k$; the sum $x+y$ lies on the bisector of the angle between them (or is $0$), so its argument is a multiple of $\frac\pi k$, and $(x+y)^k$ has argument a multiple of $\pi$, i.e. is real. $\blacksquare$

hmmt-feb-2005-team2-09.title: Reduce to $z=y/x$
hmmt-feb-2005-team2-09.body:
Let $z=\frac yx$, a root of unity with $z\ne1$, so $|z|=1$ and $x+y=x(1+z)$.

($\Rightarrow$) If $x+y$ is a root of unity then $|x+y|=1$, so $|1+z|=1$. Then $1=|1+z|^2=(1+z)(1+\bar z)=2+z+\bar z$, so $\operatorname{Re}z=-\frac12$, and with $|z|=1$ this gives $z=e^{\pm2\pi i/3}$, a cube root of unity.

($\Leftarrow$) If $z$ is a cube root of unity with $z\ne1$, then $1+z+z^2=0$, so $1+z=-z^2$ and $x+y=-xz^2$, a product of roots of unity (and $-1$), hence a root of unity. $\blacksquare$

hmmt-feb-2005-team2-10.title: Algebraic proof
hmmt-feb-2005-team2-10.body:
($\Leftarrow$) If, say, $x+y=0$, then $x+y+z=z$ is a root of unity.

($\Rightarrow$) Let $w=x+y+z$ be a root of unity, so all of $x,y,z,w$ have absolute value $1$ and $\bar x=\frac1x$ etc. Conjugating $w=x+y+z$: $\frac1w=\frac1x+\frac1y+\frac1z=\frac{xy+yz+zx}{xyz}$, so $xy+yz+zx=\frac{xyz}w$. Then
$$(w-x)(w-y)(w-z)=w^3-w^2(x+y+z)+w(xy+yz+zx)-xyz=w^3-w^3+xyz-xyz=0.$$
So $w=x$, $w=y$ or $w=z$; say $w=z$. Then $x+y+z=z$, i.e. $x+y=0$. (Similarly in the other cases we get $y+z=0$ or $z+x=0$.) $\blacksquare$

hmmt-feb-2005-team2-11.title: Polynomial factorization
hmmt-feb-2005-team2-11.body:
Subtract $1$ from all elements: $S'=S-1\subset\{0,\dots,11\}$ contains $0$, and if $T'$ is the set of tile minima (shifted likewise), then every number $0,\dots,11$ is written exactly once as $s+t$ with $s\in S'$, $t\in T'$. With $P(x)=\sum_{s\in S'}x^s$ and $Q(x)=\sum_{t\in T'}x^t$ this says
$$P(x)Q(x)=1+x+\cdots+x^{11}=\Phi_2\Phi_3\Phi_4\Phi_6\Phi_{12},$$
where $\Phi_2=1+x$, $\Phi_3=1+x+x^2$, $\Phi_4=1+x^2$, $\Phi_6=1-x+x^2$, $\Phi_{12}=1-x^2+x^4$ (irreducible over $\mathbb Z$). So $P$ is a product of a subset of these five factors, and $Q$ is the product of the rest: $2^5=32$ candidate pairs, and we need both products to have all coefficients in $\{0,1\}$. Checking the $32$ subsets (equivalently running through the greedy tiling, where the smallest uncovered number must start the next tile) leaves exactly $16$ sets $S$. They come in pairs $S\leftrightarrow T$ (a set and its set of tile minima), shown with $T$ in brackets:

- $\{1\}$ $[\{1,\dots,12\}]$,
- $\{1,2\}$ $[\{1,3,5,7,9,11\}]$,
- $\{1,3\}$ $[\{1,2,5,6,9,10\}]$,
- $\{1,4\}$ $[\{1,2,3,7,8,9\}]$,
- $\{1,7\}$ $[\{1,\dots,6\}]$,
- $\{1,2,3\}$ $[\{1,4,7,10\}]$,
- $\{1,3,5\}$ $[\{1,2,7,8\}]$,
- $\{1,5,9\}$ $[\{1,2,3,4\}]$,

and the other eight are the $T$'s: $\{1,\dots,12\}$, $\{1,3,5,7,9,11\}$, $\{1,2,5,6,9,10\}$, $\{1,2,3,7,8,9\}$, $\{1,\dots,6\}$, $\{1,4,7,10\}$, $\{1,2,7,8\}$, $\{1,2,3,4\}$. For example $S=\{1,2,7,8\}$ tiles with tile minima $1,3,5$: $\{1,2,7,8\},\{3,4,9,10\},\{5,6,11,12\}$.

(All $16$ sets were also confirmed by an exhaustive check of the subsets of $\{1,\dots,12\}$ containing $1$.)

hmmt-feb-2005-team2-12.title: An involution on tilings
hmmt-feb-2005-team2-12.body:
Normalize: every class of sets $S$ has a unique representative with $\min S=0$, so we count sets $S\ni0$ that tile $A$ (up to the fixed translation of $A$ by $-\min A$ we may also assume $\min A=0$). Since $A$ is finite, any tiling is unique (previous argument: the smallest uncovered element forces the next tile). If $S$ tiles $A$, let $T=\{t_0=0<t_1<\cdots\}$ be the set of translations (the minima of the tiles), so $A$ is the disjoint union of $S+t$ ($t\in T$): every element of $A$ is written uniquely as $s+t$, $s\in S$, $t\in T$.

By symmetry of this description, $A$ is also the disjoint union of the sets $T+s$ ($s\in S$), so $T$ tiles $A$ too, with the tile-position set $S$. Define $\iota(S)=T$ ($T$ contains $0$ and is normalized). Then $\iota(T)=S$ by uniqueness of the tiling, so $\iota$ is an involution on the sets tiling $A$.

It has no fixed point: suppose $T=S$. Since $A$ has more than one element, $|S|\ge2$ (if $|S|=1$ then $T=A\ne S$), so $S$ has an element $s_1\ne0$ and $0\in S$. Then $0+s_1=s_1+0$ are two representations of the element $s_1$ of $A$ as (element of $S$)+(element of $T$), contradicting uniqueness. So the sets tiling $A$ split into pairs $\{S,\iota(S)\}$, and their number is even. $\blacksquare$

hmmt-feb-2005-team2-13.title: An example
hmmt-feb-2005-team2-13.body:
Take $S=\{1,3,4,6\}$.

*It tiles $\mathbb Z$.* Its elements are distinct modulo $4$ ($1,3,0,2$), so $\mathbb Z=\bigsqcup_{j\in\mathbb Z}(S+4j)$.

*It does not tile $\mathbb N$.* In a tiling of $\mathbb N$ by translates $S+t$ ($t\ge0$ since the tiles must lie in $\mathbb N$), the element $1$ lies in a tile with minimum $1$ (it is the least element of $\mathbb N$), so $\{1,3,4,6\}$ is a tile. The element $2$ is in a different tile $S+t$; $2=t+1$ gives $t=1$ and $S+1=\{2,4,5,7\}$, which overlaps the first tile at $4$; $2=t+3$ gives $t=-1<0$, $2=t+4$ gives $t=-2$, $2=t+6$ gives $t=-4$, all impossible. So there is no tiling.

(Another example is $\{1,2,6\}$.)

hmmt-feb-2005-team2-14.title: Gaps between cubes grow
hmmt-feb-2005-team2-14.body: Let $a=\max S-\min S$ and suppose $S$ has more than one element, so $a>0$. In a tiling of the set of cubes $\{n^3:n\in\mathbb Z\}$, the tile containing $b^3$ is a translate of $S$ consisting entirely of cubes, all within distance $a$ of $b^3$. For all sufficiently large $b$, the neighboring cubes are farther away than $a$: $(b+1)^3-b^3=3b^2+3b+1>a$ and $b^3-(b-1)^3=3b^2-3b+1>a$. So the only cube in $[b^3-a,b^3+a]$ is $b^3$ itself, and the tile containing $b^3$ has only one element. But every tile is a translate of $S$ and has $|S|\ge2$ elements, a contradiction. Hence $|S|=1$. $\blacksquare$

hmmt-feb-2005-team2-15.title: Casework on the smallest elements
hmmt-feb-2005-team2-15.body:
Normalize $\min S=0$ and suppose $|S|\ge2$. Tiles are translates $t+S$. The tile containing $3$ has $3$ as its minimum (it is the smallest odd prime): $S_0=3+S$. Every element $s\in S$ is even, since $3+s$ is an odd prime. Let $s_1>0$ be the second-smallest element of $S$.

- $s_1=2$: then $3,5\in S_0$. The prime $7$ is either in $S_0$ (iff $4\in S$) or the minimum of its own tile $S_1=7+S\ni 9$ (as $2\in S$), but $9$ is not prime, a contradiction. If $4\in S$, then $S_0\supseteq\{3,5,7\}$ and every other tile has minimum $p\ge11$ and contains $p,p+2,p+4$; one of three numbers $p,p+2,p+4$ is divisible by $3$ and exceeds $3$, so it is not prime. Contradiction.
- $s_1=4$: then $7\in S_0$, and $5$ is not in $S_0$ (that would need $2\in S$), so $5$ is the minimum of its tile $5+S\ni9$, not prime. Contradiction.
- $s_1\ge6$: the primes $5$ and $7$ are not in $S_0$ (that needs $2,4\in S$), and $7\notin5+S$ (needs $2\in S$), so $5$ and $7$ are minima of their own tiles. Then $3+s_1,\ 5+s_1,\ 7+s_1$ are all prime, three numbers of the form $p,p+2,p+4$ larger than $3$, one of which is divisible by $3$. Contradiction.

So $S$ has only one element. $\blacksquare$
